blocks.text: The chapter moves from public conduct to a summary of salvation and back to practical conduct. Its instructions for obedience, gentleness, and good works are framed by the claim that salvation rests on mercy and grace rather than on righteous works people have done. Good works therefore appear as the fitting fruit of mercy, not as the means of earning it.

The word translated “love toward man” carries the sense of humane kindness or love for humanity. In verses 4–7, this kindness marks the turn from the shared description of a former life to mercy, renewal by the Holy Spirit, justification by grace, and hope. The “washing of regeneration” has been read in overlapping ways—such as baptismal, conversion-initiation, new-creation, or metaphorical—so the phrase alone should not be made to settle every later sacramental question.

The letter rejects foolish controversies, genealogies, quarrels, and disputes about law as unprofitable, but it does not provide enough detail to identify a particular movement or to stigmatize Jewish study, scholarship, or sincere disagreement. Likewise, the term in verse 10 concerns a divisive or factional person in this setting; it should not simply be equated with every later technical use of “heretic.” The stated process is two warnings followed by refusal, not a complete procedure for discipline.

The closing notices place the teaching about good works in practical community life: Artemas or Tychicus may replace Titus, Titus is to join the writer at Nicopolis for the winter, and Zenas and Apollos are to be supplied for their journey. The passage does not complete the picture: the identities, routes, exact location of Nicopolis, dates, and outcomes remain uncertain. What it does make clear is the community’s responsibility to meet urgent needs so that its good works are not fruitless.
The surviving Codex Vaticanus ends before the Pastoral Epistles, so it is not a manuscript witness to Titus.
